# Verification, Feedback, and Learning {#sec-feedback-verification-trust}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"Program testing can be used to show the presence of bugs, but never to show their absence!"*
>
>  –   Edsger W. Dijkstra, *Notes on Structured Programming* (1970) [@Dijkstra1970Notes]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** Dijkstra's warning separates an architectural check from the broader claims we might be tempted to attach to it. Passing our testbenches or simulations only validates the specific conditions and workloads we exercised. Conversely, a single failed assertion can decisively shatter a bounded claim about our design's correctness.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
When we receive signals from our AI-assisted design workflows, what do they actually tell us about our chosen actions, hardware artifacts, assumptions, or performance results? More importantly, how should we adapt our architectural strategies based on that feedback?
:::

A returned signal never explains itself. In computer architecture, we receive complex signals from our EDA tools, simulation environments, human peer reviews, machine learning models, and finally from our deployed silicon. Verification performs the critical, claim-specific work of determining whether a given return is actually trustworthy and what architectural decisions it can legitimately support. We use empirical checks to qualify the observed or computed quantities we gather from benchmark runs, experiments, FPGA prototypes, or production systems. When we perform dynamic verification, we use targeted tests, cycle-accurate simulation, or hardware emulation to exercise our design and observe its specific behaviors. On the other hand, formal methods allow us to use mathematical models and logic to establish the rigorous status of a property over a model under clearly stated assumptions [@Clarke2018ModelChecking]. We must treat these approaches as complementary, rather than interchangeable. Feedback is how we interpret these qualified results for a specific design component and identify our next justified engineering action. Learning then captures what our team improves or retains based on that interpretation. A given return might report a performance measurement, expose a deep pipeline failure, localize a critical path bottleneck, challenge a microarchitectural rationale, or simply leave a design question unresolved. Ultimately, we can only justify a recorded update to our designs when we explicitly document what tool produced the return, which hardware component it refers to, when it was obtained, and exactly what kind of architectural pivot it supports.

Our architectural studies inherently combine a massive variety of inputs: empirical measurements, formal verification bounds, trace-driven simulations, physical layout analysis, predictive model scores, peer design reviews, and real-world operational observations. We cannot assume these heterogeneous signals share a universal definition of a *pass*, a uniform type of uncertainty, or a single scope. As architects, we must qualify every return against the precise hardware property it attempts to address. We have to meticulously compare apples to apples, explicitly expose the corner cases that remain unchecked, and actively route our results into the design process rather than passively letting the signal dictate its own application.

Today, our AI generators might synthesize hardware candidates incredibly fast, our predictors might score them instantly, and our optimizers might search vast design spaces directly against imperfect power or area proxies. We also know that generated LLM explanations often sound far more certain than our actual measurements can justify. However, this profound acceleration in our workflows does not absolve us of our strict, property-specific verification obligations. Every single generated candidate still demands a rigorous check against a declared architectural property, an adequate golden reference model or expected-result rule, explicitly recorded environmental conditions, and comprehensive test coverage. Furthermore, when we use AI to generate our tests or assertions, we immediately create new questions about the adequacy of those very checks. We are finding that while our capacity for candidate production can scale exponentially, the human-in-the-loop work required to rigorously qualify a result remains our fundamental bottleneck. Ultimately, AI fundamentally accelerates our process, but it does not change the high standard of what a valid computer architecture result must contain.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, we can:

- Qualify tool returns by type and status to preserve data lineage.
- Construct matched architectural comparisons to isolate design impact.
- Interpret formal bounds and empirical uncertainty without overextending claims.
- Validate fast proxy metrics against bias, confounding, and selection risks.
- Apply qualified feedback to guide actions without treating every return as ML training data.
:::

## From Tool Return to Qualified Action {#sec-from-feedback-to-decision}

As we saw in @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces, our design environment meticulously logs whether our request was valid, what executed, what failed, which artifacts we got back, and the state and cost associated with the attempt. In this chapter, we pick up right where that record leaves off. We need to determine if a returned metric is actually valid for the architectural property we want to evaluate. From there, we must figure out exactly what kind of claim our qualified result can support, and ultimately, which technical decisions we are now ready to make.

Any signal we get back from our tools can only justify changing our architecture if we build a solid sequence of claims. First, we qualify the result to establish exactly what it means. Once we have that qualified result, we can use it to support a strictly bounded claim about our design. Only then does a specific architectural action become eligible, allowing us to safely lock in a design change or a learned lesson. We cannot skip steps here; a flaw early in this sequence will doom everything that follows.

We should also remember that not every tool returns a hard measurement. We might receive a design review rationale, a model critique, a formal proof status, a counterexample, or even just a compiler warning. These qualitative outputs are incredibly useful to our design process, provided we carefully record their source, target, scope, timing, and inherent limitations. On the other hand, whenever we do get a raw numerical return, we must rigorously qualify it before we can trust it enough to compare different microarchitectural choices.

We have all seen tool setups fail, but we must recognize that a failed setup is not just a poor measurement of our candidate architecture – it gives us absolutely no measurement at all. Even if our EDA process exits cleanly, it might still hand us a partial timing report, omit a crucial metric, report power in the wrong units, or mistakenly parse an unfamiliar warning as a success. Conversely, a perfectly complete return might accurately report a genuine design rule or timing violation. Because of these nuances, we must always preserve the raw execution status intact so our interpretation phase can accurately distinguish between a tool failure and an architectural failure.

When an evaluation run doesn't finish, we don't necessarily have to throw away every artifact it generated, but we must tie any salvage operation to a specific architectural claim. We can only push an individual metric or artifact forward into qualification if our run specifications treat it as independently complete. Its extraction and lineage must be flawless, we must be certain that the premature termination didn't alter its meaning or observation window, and our architectural claim cannot depend on any state that went missing. If any of these conditions fail, we must quarantine that artifact along with the failed run. Furthermore, successfully salvaging a single data point does not suddenly make our timed-out or incomplete attempt "complete." Every other claim we hoped to evaluate remains strictly unresolved.

As architects reviewing these results, we must carefully separate five distinct questions. First, did our requested simulation or synthesis run actually execute? Second, is the artifact we got back structurally and semantically valid for the next step in our toolchain? Third, is the measurement or formal verification result actually valid under the conditions we stated? Fourth, which specific design requirement does this result satisfy or contradict, and what parts of our architecture remain untested? Finally, what concrete architectural conclusion or revision can we confidently support? Earning a "yes" to any one of these questions never automatically guarantees a "yes" to the ones that follow.

Consider what happens when we generate an RTL block. The generation step might complete successfully and hand us the RTL, some log files, and a preliminary timing report. However, even if that RTL parses perfectly, it might fail elaboration, struggle with library binding, or trip up on a downstream interface check. If that happens, the artifact is functionally invalid for the rest of our tool path. Even if the design does elaborate, our timing report might leave critical endpoints unconstrained, or it might have run in the wrong operating mode or process corner, rendering the data entirely invalid for our timing claims. Furthermore, even a perfectly qualified timing result only proves that we met that specific timing requirement. Our power consumption, functional correctness, and security properties remain completely uncovered, meaning we can never select our final architecture based on timing alone.

Ultimately, any signal we extract from our tools only gains real meaning as we push it through distinct, claim-specific qualifications (@fig-evidence-flow). The side routes in this process are critical to our workflow. If we get an incomplete return, we must loop back to fix our execution environment; if we fail an invalid comparison or property check, we have to step back and rethink how we formulated our architectural study.

![**A tool return gains meaning through claim-specific qualification.** Our

to support a comparative claim, we add a matched comparator; our formal and other

Our checks establish the absolute limits of what a result can tell us. Crucially, the feedback we gather does not automatically prescribe its own architectural update. Figuring out which specific design object needs our attention depends entirely on what produced the return, because our various simulation and synthesis tools expose fundamentally different properties, capabilities, and limitations.
## Sources of Returned Signals

In our architecture design workflows, we gather signals from human reviewers, simulation tools, learned models, and deployed silicon. However, no single source gives us the complete picture with immediate, precisely localized, and decision-relevant coverage. Because each source has unique blind spots, we must qualify these signals downstream rather than relying on a single preferred oracle (@tbl-feedback-sources).

| **Signal source** | **Common form** | **Timing and locality** | **Main quality question** |
|  –  |  –  |  –  |  –  |
| Human reviewer | Critique, rationale, missing constraint, or priority judgment. | Intermittent and often context-rich; locality depends on the review. | Does the reviewer have the relevant context, expertise, and authority, and is the rationale recorded? |
| Architecture tool or experiment | Scalar, trace, report, counterexample, diagnostic, or proof status. | Immediate to multi-day; may identify one path or only a terminal outcome. | Which property did the tool observe, under which conditions, with what coverage and error? |
| Learned model or method | Prediction, ranking, score, critique, or explanation. | Usually fast and dense; often tied to the supplied representation. | Does the predicted score agree with stronger checks in the region being used, and which assumptions does it share with the producer? |
| Deployed system or silicon | Telemetry, characterization result, incident, or user-visible symptom. | Delayed and sparse; often system-level rather than component-local. | Which population, version, workload, and unobserved causes limit the inference? |

: **Returned signals differ in form, timing, and locality.** We must determine whether a given signal is fit for the architectural learning or revision we expect it to support.
{#tbl-feedback-sources tbl-colwidths="[18,25,27,30]"}

As architects, we should carefully select and qualify a source based on the specific property we are evaluating and the action we plan to take. We cannot simply treat the speed, density, or directness of an observation as a proxy for its evidentiary quality.

Consider how a delayed signal often reveals a final outcome without teaching us how to fix the underlying design. For instance, a grueling three-day place-and-route and timing run might clearly show that our candidate missed timing. Unfortunately, that terminal result does not tell us which of our thousands of microarchitectural or synthesis choices actually caused the violation. To meaningfully revise our design, we need signals at the right locality – such as path slack explicitly linked to the exact graph node, parameter, or RTL transformation that we just changed.

We can draw a useful precedent from feedback engineering, which distinguishes whether the state required for a corrective action is actually observable from the design of the action itself, while treating delay as an inherent part of the feedback path [@AstromMurray2008FeedbackSystems]. In our context, a multi-day simulation or synthesis run can leave the root cause of a failure only partially observable, even when the final chip-level outcome is painfully clear. While we do not model architectural design search as a simple linear controller, we borrow a crucial lesson: the availability and latency of our signals strictly dictate which design corrections we can justify.

When handling these delayed results, we must start with strict lineage tracking rather than jumping straight to causal attribution. We need to bind every returned signal to our exact design candidate, parent actions, represented state, timing constraints, EDA tool versions, random seeds, simulation checkpoints, and the specific workloads that produced it. Of course, lineage alone does not completely qualify the return. Provided our execution, setup, extraction, and checking conditions remain valid, a terminal result firmly establishes that our candidate missed timing under those exact parameters. However, it still does not tell us which earlier architectural decision caused the miss.

Our next step is to perform a distinguishing comparison. We must dive into path endpoints, constraint coverage, routing congestion, power-density maps, and the structural differences between our current candidate and its parent or a matched sibling. If we uncover a stale constraint or a broken simulation setup, we route our revisions back to the environment or representation. On the other hand, if we see repeated failures across a matched class of design proposals – after verifying our shared setups – we can justify reopening our methodology to ask whether our representation, constraints, or proposal generation process needs an overhaul. Only when our comparison isolates a localized mechanism can we confidently justify a specific RTL or architectural revision. If our diagnostics cannot separate these possibilities, we should preserve the terminal outcome and leave the mechanism unresolved, rather than arbitrarily slapping a negative label on every upstream action.

Deployment feedback follows the exact same rule. A production incident attaches first to the shipped silicon, system software, customer workload, and the specific operating conditions present at the time. While those extreme deployment conditions might reopen an earlier architectural claim, the production symptom itself does not identify the responsible design choice until we can support that attribution with an additional, targeted diagnostic or comparison.

Naturally, dense and immediate feedback is much easier for our methodologies to learn from, but we must remember that it is often just a proxy. The signals that observe our most decision-relevant properties – like silicon-accurate power or full-system performance – are inevitably slower, vastly more expensive, and far less frequent. We can use fast proxy signals to guide our design search, but only within their rigorously validated range, while relying on slower, less frequent sign-off checks to test the properties our proxies omit. Consequently, we must carefully qualify every signal in our workflow by its latency, spatial granularity, execution cost, inherent uncertainty, and the time required for interpretation and review.

While empirical returns follow this primary qualification path, our next challenge is determining whether a given numerical value is even eligible to enter the rigorous comparisons that our architectural claims require.
## Qualifying Empirical Measurements

When we evaluate a computer architecture, an empirical measurement represents an observed or computed quantity – whether extracted from a simulation run, a synthesis implementation flow, a silicon prototype, or a deployed system under tightly recorded conditions. We must recognize that any such measurement carries inherent sampling variation, run-to-run variability, numerical tolerance, and underlying model error. We strictly differentiate these practical limits from the absolute logical certainty of a formal verification result.

To trust our architectural evaluations, we require our measurement records to definitively answer six critical questions (@tbl-measurement-record).

| **Record Element** | **Question the record must answer** |
|  –  |  –  |
| **Candidate identity** | Which design revision, hardware configuration, software state, and workload produced the value? |
| **Quantity and unit** | What architectural metric was measured or computed, how did we aggregate it, and in what unit? |
| **Conditions** | Which simulation tool, power/timing model, corner, RNG seed, and operating conditions apply to this run? |
| **Extraction status** | Did the expected output artifact exist, parse successfully under our declared schema, and retain unfamiliar warnings? |
| **Variation and error** | What repetitions, trace sampling method, numerical tolerance, modeling error, or known bound restricts the value? |
| **Source record** | Which returned artifact and execution attempt support this metric, and can we fully recover the value from them? |

: **A measurement needs identity, meaning, conditions, and limits.** These record elements test whether our execution trace provides sufficient evidence for the architectural comparison we intend to make.
{#tbl-measurement-record tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

We only allow a returned value to enter our design comparisons when these six elements make the data interpretable, establish its boundaries, and guarantee its recoverability from the original execution attempt. We treat these requirements together as a strict admission test rather than a set of independent quality scores. Crucially, passing this test does not automatically validate our architectural comparison; it simply qualifies the measured value as eligible to participate in one.

When we analyze sampled workloads or iterate through repeated physical design flows, our execution record must also explicitly specify the unit of observation, the target instruction population, the trace sampling window, our aggregation method, and any dependence structure. We ensure that missing or censored observations remain visible instead of quietly disappearing from our aggregated metrics. By rigorously tracking these parameters, we separate a merely mathematically correct computation from a robust estimate that authentically represents the workload population and drives the architectural decisions we are actually making.

Our simulation and synthesis environments provide the raw returned artifacts, extraction statuses, recorded operating conditions, and precise data lineage. We cannot rely on measurement qualification to magically reconstruct missing RTL versions or retroactively rerun a log parser. Instead, qualification asks whether our specified quantity, aggregation strategy, error margins, chosen comparator, and checking scope render the extracted metric genuinely usable for architectural evaluation. If we find missing execution parameters, we must repair our experimental environment. Conversely, if we uncover inadequate trace observations or fundamentally flawed design comparisons, we must overhaul the study itself.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="A returned value must qualify before it becomes feedback"}
**Context.** Imagine we are evaluating a prospective larger-L2 cache configuration running a fixed XR workload under a specific software state. One of our illustrative simulation attempts ends in a stale-state setup failure. A subsequent summary report provides a performance value but entirely omits the raw simulation artifacts, parser status, and data lineage. In our methodology, neither scenario constitutes retained execution evidence.

**Required record.** For rigorous qualification, we need the exact design candidate, workload trace, software stack, simulation tool, and analytical model identity. We also require the terminal status, raw return data, extraction status, units, operating conditions, and the specific uncertainty or bound that limits how we can use the value.

**Action.** We must route the stale-state failure back for environment repair while retaining its recorded failure class. We keep the subsequent unverified value strictly unqualified until we can supply its missing record. Importantly, we do not reject any architectural candidate based on either flawed case.

**Takeaway.** Mere chronological progress does not transform an infrastructure failure or an unrecoverable data summary into valid architectural design evidence.
:::

Until our execution records fully qualify, we cannot support any claims about a design candidate's outcome or its underlying architectural mechanisms. Once we qualify a measurement, it safely enters the rigorous comparisons demanded by our core architecture questions. Ultimately, qualification establishes the precise meaning of a single returned value, whereas comparison reveals the true architectural differences between our proposed candidate and a declared baseline alternative under carefully matched conditions.

We must also remember that empirical uncertainty and formal proof status answer fundamentally different questions. An empirical confidence interval summarizes hardware variation under a specific sampling and repetition procedure. How we interpret it depends heavily on the target instruction population, our chosen statistic, dependence structures, modeling errors, and required decision margins. In contrast, a formal verification result is never just a narrow empirical interval – it carries absolutely no sampling confidence level. Instead, it reports a definitive logical outcome for a mathematically stated property, machine model, and set of assumptions. While solver timeouts, proof depth boundaries, and memory constraints might limit a formal proof's scope or completion, they never degrade its statistical confidence. Therefore, before we resume any architectural comparison, our formal returns demand their own parallel qualification path that strictly evaluates the stated property, the formal model, the underlying assumptions, and the ultimate proof scope.
## Formal Verification and Its Scope

### Formal Status and Counterexamples

We evaluate formal verification along the same qualification path as we do our empirical measurements, even though formal methods do not inherently require a matched comparator. We always anchor a formal status on three core components. First, our *property* explicitly states the architectural behavior we need to verify. Second, our *model* precisely defines the state, transitions, and specific artifacts over which we interpret that property. Finally, our *assumptions* carefully constrain the inputs, environmental behaviors, resets, clock domains, protocols, and any neighboring components. For our formal results to carry real meaning, we must carry all three elements together. If we construct a proof over an inaccurate model or force an impossible assumption, we might generate a logically sound result that is ultimately useless for our architectural goals.

We often find that the model we actually check differs from the raw RTL or implementation artifact outlined in our architecture claims. Processes like elaboration, extraction, and abstraction frequently add or discard specific behaviors to make the proof tractable. Consequently, our results must explicitly state the exact correspondence our verification flow preserves between the abstract model and the final artifact, justifying why this relationship successfully maps the proved property back to our silicon [@Clarke2018ModelChecking].

We must also trust our checking base – the sequence of steps and components that transform our architectural artifact and its requirements into the mathematical problem the solver evaluates. Our documentation must rigorously identify the elaboration or model extraction procedures, property translations, relevant libraries and scripts, the specific solver or proof checker used, and any available certificate or replay path. We can easily produce a logically valid proof for a mistranslated property or an improperly extracted model, only to fail the underlying architecture requirement. Whenever our tooling yields a checkable proof certificate or replay artifact, we should diligently retain it; conversely, if a tool offers no such artifact, we must avoid implying that one exists in our records.

We must ensure our project records clearly distinguish whether the checker produced a complete proof, generated a counterexample, reached a bounded-only result, or simply remained inconclusive. Each distinct status dictates a very specific set of next actions for our engineering teams. We cannot simply relabel one result as another just because we are under pressure to reach closure.

When examining counterexamples, we need to make one critical distinction before we begin any repairs. In counterexample-guided abstraction refinement (CEGAR), we often encounter spurious counterexamples that exist solely because our abstract model permits behaviors inherently blocked by the concrete hardware; these traces guide us in refining the abstraction itself [@ClarkeEtAl2000CEGAR]. They do not prove our design is fundamentally flawed. However, if a trace survives our concretization process and setup reviews, it likely exposes a genuine architectural defect or an incorrectly specified requirement. We must treat CEGAR as a highly specific formal-verification procedure, rather than just a generic buzzword for any feedback loop. Ultimately, the exact nature of the counterexample dictates whether we must repair our abstraction, rethink our hardware design, or rewrite our requirement.

### Bounds, Progress, and Property Strength

When we utilize bounded model checking, we restrict our search space to modeled traces extending through a finite bound $k$ under our stated assumptions [@BiereEtAl1999BMC]. If we fail to find a counterexample within this limit $k$, we still cannot definitively rule out a deeper failure later in execution. To claim unbounded safety, we must either provide a rigorous completeness argument or deploy an unbounded method like induction or property-directed reachability techniques (such as IC3) [@Bradley2011IC3; @EenEtAl2011PDR]. Even after achieving an unbounded proof, we must remember that our result only validates the specifically stated property across our modeled transition system and its localized assumptions.

We must carefully distinguish between safety and liveness claims in our architectures. A safety property strictly excludes negative behaviors – for instance, preventing two disparate requesters from simultaneously holding exclusive ownership of a single cache line. Yet, proving this safety property without bounds still tells us nothing about system progress. To guarantee progress, we use liveness properties, which mandate that an accepted request will eventually receive a proper response [@AlpernSchneider1985Liveness; @Clarke2018ModelChecking]. While a bounded check might expose a stalled execution or a localized deadlock within our search horizon, it cannot prove that our system remains free from starvation or permanent deadlock over infinite time. For any unbounded progress claim, we require a liveness-capable proof or a rigorously justified reduction. Crucially, we must retain the specific fairness assumptions that preclude actions from being indefinitely postponed; if we adopt unrealistic fairness assumptions, we risk masking severe architectural progress defects. Therefore, our final results must transparently record the property class, our chosen fairness assumptions, the precise proof method, and any specific bounds or reductions we applied.

We must remain vigilant against properties passing without genuinely checking our intended behaviors. We encounter *vacuity* when the condition meant to trigger a property never actually occurs, making the logical implication vacuously true [@BeerEtAl2001Vacuity; @Clarke2018ModelChecking]. Even a nonvacuous property can be structurally weak: it might tolerate a response arriving thousands of cycles late, omit mutual exclusivity constraints, ignore reset sequencing entirely, or monitor only one requester while leaving others unconstrained. To combat this, we exercise our properties using cover statements, verifying reachable triggers, checking against known positive and negative cases, applying mutation testing, and constantly reviewing them against the high-level architectural requirements they are supposed to encode. While modern frameworks like AssertLLM can automatically generate SystemVerilog assertions from our design specifications and verify them against our golden register-transfer-level (RTL) models using formal property verification [@FangEtAl2025AssertLLM], we remain vulnerable. If both our RTL and our generated assertions inherit the identical missing requirement, a clean proof tells us absolutely nothing about the omitted architectural behavior.

We must treat these generated assertions as critical verification artifacts that demand strict qualification in their own right. Recent studies of LLM assertion generation demonstrate that general-purpose models often produce substantial fractions of syntactically and semantically invalid assertions; although task-specific, fine-tuned models markedly improve performance across those two dimensions [@PulavarthiEtAl2025AssertionGeneration]. Regardless of their origin, we must rigorously verify their syntax and elaboration, assess their semantic strength, confirm their coverage of our intended architectural properties, and evaluate whether they successfully trap intentionally seeded bugs or known historical defects. Although these robust checks make automated assertion generation significantly more useful in our design flows, they can never guarantee that our resulting property set is mathematically or architecturally complete.

### Equivalence, Refinement, and Composition

When we employ equivalence checking, we are fundamentally asking whether two discrete artifacts faithfully preserve a declared structural or behavioral relation. We often use combinational equivalence to pair state elements as structural cut points, allowing us to easily compare the combinational logic sandwiched between them. However, we must escalate to sequential equivalence whenever our architectural transformations – such as aggressive retiming, pipelined latency adjustments, the insertion of additional state, or modifications to reset mappings – alter the direct correspondence across state or time boundaries. We must keep in mind that neither technique proves that our reference artifact actually embodies the intended architecture [@Kropf1999FormalVerification].

We also find that strict equivalence is often far too rigid, particularly when our RTL implementations intentionally introduce microarchitectural details or permit fewer non-deterministic behaviors than our high-level specifications. In these cases, we rely on a refinement check, asking instead whether every implementation behavior allowed by our mapping firmly respects the broader specification. Because we routinely decompose large, unwieldy proofs by component, we frequently rely on assume-guarantee reasoning. Under this framework, each individual block proves its guarantee only as long as its surrounding environment satisfies a set of explicitly named assumptions; our overall system composition remains sound only if the neighboring blocks' guarantees successfully discharge those assumptions [@BenvenisteEtAl2018Contracts]. We must never assume a localized block proof silently scales into a whole-system proof. Consequently, our refinement mappings, precise component boundaries, interface assumptions, and any unproved remainders must all be documented as integral parts of our final verification result.

### Formal and Dynamic Coverage

As architecture reviewers, we must be able to seamlessly trace every core requirement directly to the specific formal property or relation designed to cover it. Our documentation must transparently link the original requirement source and the claimed RTL (or physical implementation artifact) back to the checked model, its governing properties, bounding assumptions, and any applied abstraction or extraction relations. Furthermore, we require explicit access to the proof method and its final status, the bound or completeness rationale, evidence defending against vacuity (such as cover traces), our chosen refinement or composition boundaries, and a frank admission of any unverified remaining logic. Even if we secure a pristine set of clean proofs, we must acknowledge that this does not inherently prove our property set is architecturally complete.

We approach dynamic simulation with a different set of claims. In our workflows, directed tests, constrained-random stimuli, coverage-guided generation, large-scale emulation, formal methods, and post-silicon testing all complement one another, primarily because exhaustive dynamic simulation remains completely infeasible for modern chips [@Kropf1999FormalVerification]. We use code coverage to report on the specific structural elements we managed to exercise during execution. Meanwhile, we leverage functional coverage to track the specific architectural events or data bins defined in our verification plans. For instance, SystemVerilog standardizes vital functional-coverage constructs like covergroups, coverpoints, discrete bins, and crosses to help us quantify our progress [@IEEE2023SystemVerilog]. Yet, we must concede that neither coverage family can mathematically guarantee what fraction of the totally reachable behavior we actually checked; conversely, our formal proofs can never verify a property we failed to write down.

When we study the catastrophic Pentium floating-point division (FDIV) failure, published accounts rigorously document both the underlying microarchitectural defect – specifically, missing lookup table entries – and the staggering \$475 million pretax charge Intel absorbed as a result [@Edelman1997PentiumDivision; @Intel1995PentiumCharge].

::: {.callout-war-story title="The Pentium FDIV bug and the limit of sampled testing"}
**The claim.** Our pre-silicon testing framework supported the implemented floating-point division behavior exclusively across the narrow slice of cases we actively exercised.

**The gap.** Five missing lookup table entries entirely escaped our simulation grids, producing mathematically incorrect results for rare operand pairs. Intel ultimately reported a \$475 million pretax charge to cover silicon replacement and associated reputational costs.

**The lesson.** Passing a suite of sampled tests cannot mathematically establish the absence of all failures in our architectures. We must deploy orthogonal formal checks whenever an architectural property demands absolute certainty.
:::

In the aftermath of such failures, we have seen formal verification evolve into the primary validation method for complex logic, such as the execution cluster within Intel's Core i7 design flow [@KaivolaEtAl2009Corei7Formal]. Having firmly established this parallel qualification path in our discipline, we can directly map the four formal result statuses to highly distinct technical actions in our engineering workflows (@tbl-formal-result-status).

| **Formal status** | **What it establishes** | **Eligible next action** |
|  –  |  –  |  –  |
| **Proved** | We have established that the declared property or equivalence holds for the recorded model and assumptions, conditional on our property translation, the model-to-artifact relationship, our trusted checking components, and an available certificate or replay path. Our proof method need not be complete for a proved result to be valid. | We record the strictly scoped result and discharge only the architectural claim explicitly covered by that property, model, assumptions, and proof mode. |
| **Counterexample** | We have found a modeled trace that violates the property. Our setup, assumptions, and concretization routines will dictate whether this trace represents a truly realizable architecture failure. | We refine our abstraction whenever CEGAR identifies a spurious trace; otherwise, we repair the design or requirement contradicted by a fully reviewed, realizable trace. |
| **Bounded-only** | We found no counterexample through our declared simulation horizon. We establish absolutely nothing beyond that bound without a separate, rigorous completeness argument. | We record the finite bound, and we either extend or change our checking method if the broader architectural claim matters, or we explicitly leave that claim open. |
| **Inconclusive** | Our solver supplied neither a proof nor a counterexample because it returned `unknown`, exhausted available compute resources, or simply failed to complete the proof procedure. | We systematically revise the abstraction, interface assumptions, proof method, or compute resource budget. We must never report this result as a pass. |

: **Our formal status determines what we can do next.** A proof discharges only its carefully scoped claim, while counterexamples, finite bounds, and incomplete proofs force us to attempt different repairs or leave our broader architectural claims open.
{#tbl-formal-result-status tbl-colwidths="[16,45,39]"}
## Building Matched Architecture Comparisons {#sec-evidence-specific-to-claim-and-scope}

When we evaluate architectural designs, our decisions typically hinge on differences rather than isolated performance numbers. If we are conducting a cache replacement study, for example, we must ask how our candidate architecture behaves relative to a baseline under identical workloads and system software states. We can certainly compare two candidate designs generated by entirely different synthesis processes, but we must recognize that the result reflects only their measured architectural difference, not necessarily the overall quality of the methodologies that produced them. Therefore, we treat the comparator as an integral part of our design claim, rather than a mere footnote appended after the fact.

Every comparison we make binds our specific candidate and comparator revisions to a single, measured difference, inextricably linking them to the precise conditions that constrain that measurement (@fig-claim-frame).

![**A comparison binds two designs to one measured difference and its limits.** We evaluate our candidate and comparator designs for the exact same quantity and unit. Our result inherently remains conditional on the specific workload, architectural state, synthesis tool constraints, uncertainty models, and the exact property our verification check can observe.](images/F7-claim-frame){#fig-claim-frame width="100%" fig-alt="Three-column comparison frame. Candidate and comparator feed a measured quantity, difference, and uncertainty, which are bounded by workload and design state, tool conditions, and check scope."}

If we change the workload, architectural state, EDA tool constraints, uncertainty model, or even the observable hardware property, we fundamentally create an entirely new comparison – even if the center numerical value remains completely unchanged. By rigorously maintaining these bindings, we prevent ourselves from erroneously carrying a measured numerical difference over into operating conditions or architectural claims that we never actually evaluated.

For our set of matched architectural cases $c_j$, we define the fundamental paired difference as

$$
d_j = y(\text{candidate}, c_j) - y(\text{comparator}, c_j).
$$

We must explicitly state our sign convention. In our evaluations, a positive value might indicate a throughput improvement, yet simultaneously represent a severe latency regression. Whenever we report a percentage, we must clearly define its denominator. Similarly, when we present an aggregate metric, we must specify whether it represents a mean, a specific tail percentile, a maximum bound, a geometric mean, or some other statistical measure. When dealing with positive performance ratios normalized against a reference design, we rely on the geometric mean to preserve a consistent relative interpretation across an entire benchmark suite; if we were to use an arithmetic mean of those ratios, our conclusions could artificially swing depending on which architectural baseline we arbitrarily chose as the reference [@FlemingWallace1986HowNotToLie]. Unless we make and document these methodological choices clearly, we risk combining two mathematically correct numbers into a completely incoherent architectural comparison.

### Matching Factors That Can Change the Result

When setting up our experiments, we must ensure our candidate and comparator differ only in the specific architectural mechanisms we intend to evaluate. Factors such as the software workload, simulation model version, synthesis tool flags, voltage/frequency operating points, cache warmup periods, trace sampling windows, and total resource budgets can easily introduce massive performance deltas that have absolutely nothing to do with our proposed hardware change. To build a truly matched comparison, we meticulously record all of these factors rather than sloppily relying on similar output filenames or shared project directories.

We often hope that systematic modeling errors will naturally cancel out in a relative comparison. However, this cancellation only occurs if our simulator or analytical model treats the candidate and comparator identically across the specific design space region we are studying. We can sometimes use a frozen, slightly inaccurate simulator to confidently establish a rank ordering of designs even if its absolute predictions diverge from post-silicon reality. Yet, this fragile bargain completely collapses if our proposed architecture change crosses an unmodeled microarchitectural boundary or triggers a pathological behavior in only one of the candidates. Ultimately, we must treat error cancellation as a rigorous hypothesis that we actively verify, rather than a magical property we inherit simply by using the same evaluation framework [@GutierrezEtAl2014SourcesOfError; @PeherstorferWillcoxGunzburger2018Multifidelity].

### Differences and Their Uncertainty

When our synthesis flows or target workloads exhibit high variability, we rely on repeated measurements to estimate run-to-run variance. We can use paired resampling techniques to preserve the critical relationship between our matched baseline and candidate execution frames.[^fn-paired-block-resampling-c07] Crucially, the object we resample is the paired-difference sequence $d_j$, rather than treating the baseline and candidate as two independently resampled streams. The confidence interval we derive from this process inherently assumes that our sequence remains sufficiently stationary over the sampled execution region, and that our declared block length successfully captures the temporal dependence relevant to our chosen statistic. Because architectural evaluations face compounding variations from numerical tolerances, finite trace sampling, heuristic synthesis algorithms, and underlying model errors, we often require specialized statistical treatments for each. We cannot simply slap one generic error bar on our graphs and expect it to represent all of these distinct sources of architectural uncertainty.

[^fn-paired-block-resampling-c07]: **Paired block resampling**: A block bootstrap resamples contiguous segments of our paired-difference sequence. We enforcing this pairing, we keep each matched baseline and candidate case tightly bound together, while the block structure preserves local temporal dependence according to the method's underlying assumptions [@Kunsch1989BlockBootstrap].

Let us consider a hypothetical, fully retained matched simulation run where we define improvement as our baseline latency minus our candidate latency. In this framing, a positive value indicates our candidate architecture is faster. Suppose our point estimate shows a 0.3\ ms speedup, but our 95 percent confidence interval stretches from -0.1\ ms to 0.7\ ms. (Keep in mind these are invented teaching values, not empirical measurements drawn from a retained Lighthouse framework run). If our future evaluation properly retains the matched execution frame sequences and applies a rigorously declared paired block-resampling procedure, we would see that this interval spans both a minor performance regression and a much larger improvement. Because the interval crosses zero, this hypothetical comparison fundamentally leaves our architectural tail-latency question unresolved, regardless of how favorable the central point estimate might appear.

To strengthen our evaluations, we can introduce a decision margin as a secondary test. If our architectural study requires a minimum practical improvement of at least $m$ (perhaps to justify the added silicon area or power overhead), our comparison must resolve the final result relative to $m$, rather than merely checking if it is greater than zero. Whenever our measured difference falls inside the boundaries of known measurement resolution or statistical uncertainty, we must accept that the outcome remains unresolved. While we might appropriately label this scenario a tie under a strict, predeclared evaluation rule, we can never legitimately claim it as an architectural improvement.

### Controlling Confounding and Selection

Even when we build a meticulously matched comparison, our data can still inadvertently support the wrong architectural explanation. Confounding effects emerge whenever an undocumented or unintended factor could equally account for our observed performance gains. To isolate our intended microarchitectural changes from other plausible alternatives, we must routinely employ stable tool versions, rigorous ablation studies, heavily controlled matched contrasts, and exhaustive sensitivity analyses.

Selection bias introduces yet another severe pitfall in our design methodologies. If our design space exploration evaluates thousands of noisy candidate architectures and we only report the single best performer, our selected peak value inherently retains some of the statistical luck that helped it win in the first place. Simply re-evaluating the same search data does absolutely nothing to remove this bias [@SmithWinkler2006OptimizersCurse]. To validate our findings, we must conduct a fresh evaluation that measures our chosen candidate architecture against entirely new random seeds, disjoint workloads, or operating cases that played no part in the initial selection phase. This secondary evaluation forces us to answer whether our performance margin actually survives in the wild, long after our automated search process has stopped cherry-picking the winner.

Finally, we must recognize that even our most carefully matched comparison might rely on an evaluation proxy that fails to translate into a realistic, post-silicon architectural result. Moreover, a highly favorable performance outcome does not automatically prove that our proposed hardware mechanism is actually functioning the way we think it is. Therefore, we must perform rigorous proxy qualification and dedicated mechanism testing as completely separate verification steps, to be executed only after we have successfully matched all candidate and comparator conditions.
## Qualifying Proxies and Testing Explanations {#sec-proxy-mismatch-metric-gaming-and-calibration}

When we rely on a cheaper signal, it must track our target architectural quantity closely enough to support the actual design decision we are making. Furthermore, the underlying mechanism we propose must independently explain the outcome we observe. A qualified proxy is undeniably useful, but it cannot answer the mechanism question on its own.

### Qualifying a Proxy for the Decision

We use architectural proxies because they give us answers earlier and more cheaply than measuring the final quantity that ultimately matters. Metrics like estimated instructions per cycle (IPC), analytical energy models, wirelength, routing congestion, hardware utilization, and simulated cycle counts all help us rank design candidates. Yet, we must remember they remain partial measurements. The danger rapidly grows when we point an optimizer directly at these proxies. We inadvertently reward our search algorithms for finding every corner of the design space where our proxy and our intended architectural result part company.

This phenomenon is Goodhart's problem manifesting in computer architecture. A measure that originally tracked a design goal can abruptly stop tracking it once we make it our primary optimization target [@Goodhart1975MonetaryManagement; @Strathern1997Goodhart]. While AI-driven design methodologies are not unique in exposing this behavior, they fundamentally change the scale and persistence with which they search for loopholes in our evaluation metrics.

When we talk about *proxy qualification*, we must keep several relationships distinct. Numerical calibration gives us a declared mapping between our proxy outputs and much stronger reference outcomes. By contrast, confidence calibration asks whether our stated probabilities or confidence intervals actually match observed frequencies – a system-evaluation question we tackle fully in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect. To evaluate observed qualification coverage, we record our sampled dimensions, our specific test strata or cases, and the gaps between them. Ultimately, we must run separate tests to determine our held-out error, the stability of our candidate rankings, our estimation uncertainty, and the overall fitness of the proxy for our architecture decision.

We must remember that observed qualification cases and held-out agreement answer entirely separate questions (@fig-trust-calibration). Our finite test cases directly establish our confidence only at sampled points or strata across our specific workload, candidate, tool, and condition dimensions. As a result, our schematic distinctly separates these observed strata from any internal gaps, as well as from the perilous extrapolation beyond our sampled design range.

![**Discrete qualification cases leave visible gaps.** Our conceptual,
normalized curves show paired proxy and stronger-reference observations in
three sampled strata, an unsampled gap between them, and possible divergence as
our search continues beyond those strata. In our real architectural studies, we must record the specific dimensions,
sampled cases or strata, gaps, and held-out agreement; we emphasize that these curves are not
measured data.](images/F9-trust-calibration){#fig-trust-calibration width="100%"
fig-alt="Conceptual normalized plot with three separate green qualification
strata in the left-hand range. Paired proxy and stronger-reference markers
appear in each stratum, while a dashed white band marks an unsampled gap between
the first two. The curves may diverge as search continues into an unqualified
right-hand range; no plotted curve is measured data."}

An internal gap remains thoroughly unqualified even if both smooth curves happen to pass through it. We still need held-out comparisons to establish whether our estimation error and candidate ordering are actually adequate at the sampled strata. Whenever we move into that gap or venture beyond our observed range, we must perform new reference checks or provide a rigorous separate justification. The possible divergence on the right side of our plot serves as a stark, practical warning. We cannot automatically assume that a higher proxy score outside our qualified support zone translates to a stronger architecture result.

Within the computer architecture community, techniques like SMARTS and SimPoint provide specific precedents for making robust population inferences. By rigorously sampling intervals from a declared benchmark execution stream, we can confidently support quantified performance estimates for that target execution population [@WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS; @SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint]. However, that powerful result does not magically make an arbitrary held-out sample representative. When we conduct a new architecture study, we must explicitly declare our target population and rigorously justify our sampling design for it. Our inference simply does not extend to workloads, design candidates, EDA tools, or operating conditions outside the boundaries of those declarations.

We must recognize that numerical calibration and ranking fidelity answer fundamentally different questions. A numerically calibrated scalar mapping relates our proxy outputs to our heavy-weight reference outcomes under a strictly declared procedure, while a predictive interval explicitly adds a stated uncertainty model to our estimates [@ForresterSobesterKeane2008Surrogate]. On the other hand, ranking fidelity asks whether our candidate ordering actually survives the scrutiny of the stronger check. We can easily have low average error alongside entirely wrong orderings near a critical architectural decision boundary, just as we can have highly useful ordering alongside heavily biased absolute values. Proper qualification therefore reports the specific relationship our design decision requires, and it rigorously tests our proxy's error or instability against our explicitly declared margin.

Because a proxy can fail us in several distinct ways, and because each type of failure eliminates a different architectural inference, we must apply separate diagnostic tests for the six primary problems (@tbl-proxy-diagnostics).

| **Concern** | **Diagnostic check** | **What an adverse result means** |
|  –  |  –  |  –  |
| **Proxy mismatch** | We compare the proxy with a more decision-relevant measurement on matched cases. | Our available evidence does not support carrying the proxy result to the stronger architectural claim. |
| **Observed qualification coverage** | We record the workload, candidate, tool, and condition dimensions; place matched cases across sampled strata; and identify gaps our search may enter. | Our available evidence does not qualify a reported candidate outside sampled cases or inside an unqualified gap. |
| **Held-out agreement** | We measure error, ranking stability, and uncertainty against our decision margin on cases not used to fit or tune the proxy. | Our available evidence does not support reliable candidate ordering for the declared use, even at observed qualification cases. |
| **Confounding** | We hold versions and design budgets fixed, use matched contrasts, and test plausible alternative causes. | Our measured difference does not identify the proposed architectural cause. |
| **Variability** | We repeat stochastic flows or sampled workloads and report dispersion or ranking stability. | Our point estimate may fail to resolve the declared architectural margin. |
| **Selection bias** | We re-evaluate our selected candidate on fresh cases not used to choose it. | Our apparent margin may simply contain the luck that allowed the candidate to win. |

: **Each weakness requires a different diagnostic.** We cannot repair
a missing property with a mere second run, and we cannot repair an unmatched comparator by switching to a stronger tool.
{#tbl-proxy-diagnostics tbl-colwidths="[18,43,39]"}

For a proxy to be useful, it first has to actually observe the relevant property, maintain matched qualification cases exactly where our search will rely on it, and faithfully preserve the ordering our design decision needs on held-out cases. From there, we must use separate diagnostics to rule out alternative causes, isolate run-to-run variation, and identify favorable noise that might have been retained when our search selected its winner. An adverse result in any of these tests removes only the specific inference we name in the final column. It certainly does not make our other architectural diagnoses or repairs interchangeable.

When we perform robustness checks, we explicitly stress our current claim envelope rather than silently widening it. We varying workload phases, random seeds, nearby design candidates, tool or model alternatives, and process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) corners, we can easily expose a candidate ranking or performance margin that completely depends on a single favorable case. When we test sensitivity to those declared factors, it either narrows, contradicts, or vigorously supports our current architectural result. If we change our design objective or specification, we must first reopen any proxy relationships that depend on it. If our change fundamentally alters what success means for our target decision, our old qualification simply no longer answers the same question, and we absolutely must not present it as a robustness result.

We can look to the recent public debate over learned macro placement to see exactly why rigorous qualification and matched comparisons matter so much. Proxy metrics such as estimated wirelength and routing congestion do not automatically settle post-route power, performance, and area (PPA). Furthermore, public assessments of these methods have differed significantly in their EDA tool flows, baseline strengths, pretraining data, and available design artifacts [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement; @GoldieEtAl2024AlphaChipAddendum; @ChengEtAl2026UpdatedAssessment; @GoldieEtAl2024ThatChipHasSailed]. The durable lesson here is not a definitive verdict on one specific placement method. Rather, it reminds us that a proxy comparison cannot silently inherit credibility from a stronger architectural result obtained under unmatched conditions.

We must also recognize that a simulator itself can easily become the exploited reference. In their study on architecture agents, Gupta et al. showed how an optimized ChampSim build inadvertently eliminated an assertion against last-level-cache write bypassing, meaning the configuration completely failed to enforce the intended correctness constraint [@GuptaEtAl2026ArchAgent]. If we were to qualify a proxy against that flawed run, we would perfectly reproduce its blind spot. Any architectural reference check we use must stringently retain the property, configuration, and coverage we originally used to justify it.

Even perfectly qualified measurements still do not choose for us when we must balance performance, power, and area. Each discrete quantity retains its own unit and uncertainty, and our hard constraints must remain firmly separate. For any aggregate ranking we build, we must explicitly declare our normalization methods, weights, or Pareto dominance rules. If two design candidates remain nondominated, our feedback accurately exposes a fundamental architecture tradeoff, rather than artificially manufacturing a winner for us [@Deb2001MultiObjective].

### Separating the Outcome From the Mechanism

In any rigorous methodology, an outcome tells us what changed in our design, while a mechanism tells us why. Because they require entirely different comparisons and can easily reach different validation statuses, we can often find a strongly supported mechanism sitting beside an architectural outcome that our comparison leaves unresolved.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="A lower miss count is not the architecture result"}
**Context.** A future Lighthouse cache run could measure 99th-percentile frame
time and capacity misses under strictly matched workload and software conditions. We note that the
book currently reports no such execution result.

**Required distinction.** A lower miss count supports an intermediate
cache effect only after we properly qualify it. Establishing an actual frame-time outcome and
proving that fewer misses genuinely caused it require completely separate comparisons.

**Action.** We must preserve the intermediate effect if it is qualified, honestly leave the frame-time
comparison unresolved when its confidence interval crosses zero, and introduce a distinguishing
mechanism check before we let that explanation guide our next design change.

**Takeaway.** We cannot use an intermediate measurement to fill in for an unresolved
architecture outcome or a mechanism claim.
:::

The reverse scenario can also occur in our studies. A design candidate may clearly improve our measured outcome, even while our proposed explanation for the improvement completely fails. The performance gain remains a perfectly valid observation if our comparison is sound, but an unresolved or contradicted mechanism should absolutely not guide our next architectural change. A plausible analytical model explanation is merely a hypothesis; it is never a valid substitute for a rigorous contrast.

When we need useful mechanism checks, we can leverage matched workload contrasts, rigorous ablations, counterfactual configurations, detailed traces of the affected architectural events, and careful sensitivity studies around our changed parameters. We should declare these checks before we see the result whenever possible. Otherwise, we run the risk of fitting an explanation to any outcome after the fact. We can only claim a contrast identifies a cause when our architectural intervention is exceptionally well defined, and when plausible alternative execution paths are ruled out by our experimental design or bounded by explicit identification assumptions [@Pearl2009Causality]. We must ensure our resulting judgments remain separate, even when we derive them from the exact same simulation study (@tbl-outcome-mechanism).

| **Question** | **Possible status** | **Architecture example** |
|  –  |  –  |  –  |
| **Did the requested quantity change in the declared direction?** | Supported, contradicted, or unresolved within our stated comparison. | A latency confidence interval that includes zero leaves our claimed improvement entirely unresolved. |
| **Did the proposed intermediate effect occur?** | Supported, contradicted, unresolved, or simply not tested. | A qualified reduction in capacity misses strongly supports a bounded cache effect. |
| **Did that intermediate effect actually cause the outcome?** | Supported only by a distinguishing intervention or contrast under our stated identification assumptions; otherwise left unresolved. | A lower miss count alone does not establish that it caused a measured tail-latency change. |
| **What did our check fundamentally not observe?** | Explicit nonclaims. | A cache-local result does not establish system thermal behavior, voltage-droop vulnerability, functional correctness, security bounds, or system-level XR quality. |

: **Outcome and mechanism remain completely separate results.** We cannot allow a supported intermediate
effect to fill in for an unresolved architecture comparison.
{#tbl-outcome-mechanism tbl-colwidths="[26,30,44]"}

Our collected evidence does not need to resolve all of these questions together. We might resolve an outcome and an intermediate effect while leaving the proposed cause entirely open, and even a strongly supported cause cannot arbitrarily widen the set of properties our check actually observed. We can confidently use a local cache result to guide our next cache experiment, but we must not let it magically become a claim about thermal constraints, electrical limits, functional correctness, security guarantees, or whole-system behavior.

Ultimately, strictly enforcing this separation makes our negative results incredibly useful. A contradicted mechanism effectively improves our mental architecture model even when our candidate result looks favorable. A carefully resolved performance regression instantly rules out an unfruitful design direction. Similarly, an unresolved comparison cleanly reveals that our simulation observation budget or measurement plan was simply too weak. None of these outcomes represents a failed study, provided our methodological record keeps them fiercely distinct.
## Matching Checks to Claims {#sec-independent-checks-and-correlated-errors}

As architects, we know that merely supporting a difference does not equate to adequate requirement coverage. We must ensure each material architecture requirement has a suitable check path, and together, our chosen paths must fully cover the underlying claim.

When we engage in assurance engineering, we connect our claims directly to the checks and assumptions that support them [@Kelly2004GSN]. We can preserve this connection through a cumulative study record, avoiding the overhead of a second project process or the trap of reducing our results to a single confidence score. For each architectural claim, our record must name the property and scope, the check coverage and possible error direction, our shared assumptions, and the formal proof status where applicable. We must also document empirical and model uncertainty, the basis for any independence claim, explicit nonclaims, and ultimately, the consequence of being wrong.

We cannot simply average these attributes into a single metric. To increase our confidence, we must reduce or bound the relevant failure paths for a specific claim. If we see agreement between checks that share the exact same blind spot, we haven't actually reduced the risk contributed by that shared vulnerability. We must recognize that a formally proved property can easily coexist with uncertain performance profiles, incomplete workload coverage, and entirely untested security claims.

### Connecting Requirements to Checks

Passing every check we run does not automatically establish requirement satisfaction. For every declared material requirement or hard constraint in our design, we must explicitly name the artifact and its conditions, the acceptance criterion, and a check path perfectly suited to the property. We also have to track empirical uncertainty or formal status, our shared assumptions, and any uncovered remainder. If we leave a mapping missing or unqualified, that requirement remains unresolved – even if every other check passes with flying colors. And of course, passing all mapped checks still does not guarantee that our overall requirement set is complete.

When we tackle a statistical performance or reliability requirement, we can lean on a confidence interval, provided we clearly declare the target population, sampling assumptions, risk criterion, and decision margin. Some of our yield and manufacturing requirements are inherently statistical, meaning we must retain their population and variation models. Conversely, when we face a hard timing, power, or design-rule acceptance limit, we need our designated signoff method to strictly resolve the acceptance rule across named modes, corners, modeled variation, and uncertainty. We must remember that a favorable point estimate is never a hard-limit pass. If our designated analysis cannot place us safely on the acceptable side of the limit under those rigorous conditions, the requirement remains unresolved.

We can look at the unexecuted Lighthouse cache study to make these mappings concrete without inventing a candidate result.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="Our Lighthouse requirements remain unresolved for different reasons"}
**Context.** In our prospective study, we name request and interface legality, SRAM area and access time, 99th-percentile frame time, a 3\ W subsystem power target, alongside functional, protocol, security, reliability, and system-level XR behavior.

**Required checks.** To validate request legality, SRAM limits, frame time, and power, we need versioned request and artifact checks. We require complete SRAM results specifying our model, process, voltage, and temperature conditions, as well as matched frame-time measurements detailing their uncertainty, and a qualified subsystem power result. For the remaining properties, we need simulation or named formal checks that actively observe each declared requirement.

**Status.** Our prospective study currently has no translated inputs, retained SRAM or power artifacts, matched frame records, parser evidence, or uncertainty data. Consequently, those four mappings are unqualified – they are neither passes nor failures. Our functional, protocol, security, reliability, and system-level XR requirements lack any check path and remain completely uncovered. At this stage, all our candidate choices remain open.

**Takeaway.** When we hold an unqualified result, we lack the essential record needed to interpret its check. When a requirement is uncovered, we simply lack a suitable check. While human review can expose either gap in our methodology, it can never supply a missing measurement or proof.
:::

### What Different Checks Establish

Even a perfectly valid measurement might address the completely wrong property. In architecture, our syntax checks, functional simulation, model checking, performance simulation, synthesis, timing analysis, power analysis, and post-silicon characterization all answer fundamentally different questions. We shouldn't view their strength as a single, linear progression from weak to strong. For instance, a simple parser can conclusively reject an illegal request, whereas our most expensive timing run tells us absolutely nothing about functional correctness. We defining representative check boundaries, we make these mismatches explicit without implying any universal ordering (@tbl-check-scope).

| **Check class** | **What it can support within stated conditions** | **What it does not establish by itself** |
|  –  |  –  |  –  |
| **Syntax and interface** | Legal encoding, type, schema, instruction set architecture (ISA), application binary interface (ABI), or protocol form. | Functional behavior, performance, physical feasibility, or system intent. |
| **Functional simulation and testing** | Behavior for exercised stimuli and observed properties. | Unexercised behaviors, physical timing, power, or unspecified security properties. |
| **Formal property and equivalence checks** | A stated property over a modeled transition system, or a stated relation between two artifacts. | Whether the property captures intent, whether assumptions match deployment, or unrelated properties. |
| **Architecture performance and power models** | Quantities represented by the model for the declared workload and configuration. | Effects the abstraction omits or behavior outside its validated region. |
| **Implementation and physical analysis** | Timing, area, power, integrity, or rule results for the modeled design, constraints, modes, and corners. | Missing constraints, unmodeled conditions, functional intent, or manufactured variation outside the analysis. |
| **Post-silicon and operational measurement** | Behavior of sampled parts and systems under measured conditions. | Every manufactured part, workload, environment, lifetime condition, or unmeasured property. |

: **Our checks are decisive only for the properties they actually observe.** Committing more cost or placing a check later in our flow does not artificially widen that property.
{#tbl-check-scope tbl-colwidths="[22,39,39]"}

Our checks are complementary, rather than a strict hierarchy from weak to strong. We often find that a later or more expensive check settles one specific implementation property while leaving our functional intent, security postures, or earlier interface obligations completely untouched. Therefore, our architecture claims demand thorough coverage across all material properties, not merely a progression to the most expensive tool stage we have available.

We must also realize that the specific property a check observes is only half of our measurement plan. How we intend to use its result matters just as much. If we rely on a mistaken local ranking, we will waste our evaluation budget and skew which architectural candidates our search ultimately examines. Worse, if we use a mistaken result to revise a shared artifact or interface, that error can rapidly propagate across our hardware, software, verification, and integration workstreams. Consequently, our feedback plan must grow in proportion to the cost of being wrong and the sheer difficulty of reversing the result's technical consequences (@tbl-feedback-by-consequence).

| **Intended use of the result** | **Consequence if the result is wrong** | **Feedback plan should include** |
|  –  |  –  |  –  |
| **Choose the next local evaluation** | A candidate is explored unnecessarily, a promising one is deferred, or scarce tool time is spent on the wrong question. | Candidate identity, a matched comparator, known proxy limits, and enough precision to choose the next check. |
| **Revise a shared implementation or interface** | Hardware, software, verification, or integration work may inherit the error. | Relevant regression and compatibility checks, explicit shared assumptions, and a different check path for critical properties where practical. |
| **Support a high-consequence technical conclusion** | The error may survive into later work where it is expensive to find or reverse. | Checks covering each material claim, uncertainty relative to the decision margin, a sufficiently different path where shared failure matters, and explicit unmeasured properties. |

: **Our feedback plans must follow consequence and reversibility.** We shouldn't assume more costly checks are automatically more informative. Instead, our plans must comprehensively cover the claims and failure modes that matter for the result's intended use.
{#tbl-feedback-by-consequence tbl-colwidths="[27,32,41]"}

Once our results can propagate into shared artifacts or expensive downstream work, any wrong interpretation becomes remarkably harder to reverse. We must remember that having robust technical support still does not automatically authorize the resulting architectural action.

### Describing the Check and Its Limits

We frequently encounter architecture results that depend on confidential workloads, proprietary design data, or heavily customized tool flows. These results can comfortably support an internal conclusion, provided an authorized reviewer can inspect the complete record and actively challenge our methods, scope, uncertainty, and limits. However, any public claim we make must remain strictly within the bounds of what public material – or an audit by a reviewer with access to our protected records – can establish. Simply invoking confidentiality does not magically turn a production report into an independently replayable comparison.

To make our architectural checks truly reviewable, we must answer three questions that many standard tool reports omit:

- **Coverage:** Which failures can our check actually observe, and which relevant failures will leave absolutely no signal?

- **Possible error direction:** Under our declared models and conditions, do we know if the result is conservative, optimistic, or neither? We must establish this for our particular flow. A pre-route estimate is not always optimistic, and a deterministic computation does not automatically guarantee a safe bound.

  Static timing analysis perfectly illustrates why error direction is highly conditional. Cadence documents concurrent multi-mode, multi-corner analysis and statistical on-chip variation analysis in Tempus [@Cadence2021Tempus]. However, our architecture lesson here extends far beyond specific product capabilities. We might find a result is deliberately pessimistic, but that claim only applies to our explicitly declared timing mode, our specific process, voltage, and temperature corners, our derates, our constraints, and our modeled effects. A pass or failure only holds meaning within those rigorous conditions; it is never a universal bound. Sampled simulation takes a different shape entirely. A failing trace decisively rejects the exercised behavior, but a passing sample tells us nothing about unexercised stimuli or properties absent from our testbench.

- **Shared assumptions:** Which specifications, models, data, workloads, constraints, code, and tool paths do we share with the producer or with another check? Using a different program name or booting up a new model instance does not, by itself, create independence.

When we see agreement between checks, it only adds real information if our second path actually changes the relevant failure source (@fig-independent-checks). Our alternative method doesn't need to claim perfect independence. Instead, it must observe the disputed property through a sufficiently different path to meaningfully reduce any known shared failure modes.

![**Our second check adds information only when it changes the relevant failure path.** If our critic uses the same assumptions, they can easily repeat the producer's omission. A claim-specific check based on a sufficiently different model or measurement path can reduce that correlation, but we must still record its remaining shared inputs and blind spots.](images/ch7_independent_checks){#fig-independent-checks width="92%" fig-alt="Two-column diagram. A producer and critic sharing the same assumptions lead to correlated agreement. A producer and a claim-specific check with a different measurement path lead to a bounded challenge, with remaining shared assumptions explicitly retained."}

In the left path, because our candidate producer and critic use the exact same specification and model, their agreement remains inherently correlated. Conversely, in the right path, our claim-specific check observes the disputed property through a different mechanism, producing a much tighter, bounded challenge.

We must be careful not to conflate two distinct uses of a second path. When we perform an independent qualification of the same record, we are primarily challenging extraction, arithmetic, or basic bookkeeping. For example, our separate parser might recover a value from a raw report, and an independent calculation can verify its aggregation.
