However, both operations likely still inherit the original tool's underlying model, workload, and constraints. They strengthen our confidence in what the tool returned, but they completely fail to test whether the tool observed the correct physical property in the first place.

A materially different observation path challenges far more of our architectural claim. We utilizing another simulator with distinct models, a rigorous RTL property check, a physical-design measurement, or even a direct hardware observation, we might expose fundamental errors that mere record requalification cannot catch. Naturally, this new path carries its own shared assumptions that we must explicitly name. The most useful question we can ask is not whether the second path truly deserves the label *independent*. Rather, we must ask which failure source it actually changes and which vulnerabilities remain shared.

We must acknowledge that separate teams can still fail together when faced with the same hard inputs. Knight and Leveson found deeply correlated failures among independently developed program versions, proving that separate implementations do not magically guarantee independent errors [@KnightLeveson1986Multiversion]. This precise warning applies to our workflows when a generator proposes an architectural candidate and a critic challenges it. While separating the proposal from the challenge can make our assumptions much easier to inspect, it does not inherently create independent evidence. If our components share a foundation model, training data, supplied context, retrieved material, reward functions, overarching specifications, or even a basic tool path, their failures will likely remain correlated. While agreement provides useful corroboration, any strong independence claim we make must rest on a sufficiently different check, tool, evidence source, or information path – not merely on counting the number of components we deploy.

Recent developments in LLM evaluation supply a narrower, yet vital, warning for our automation pipelines. Experiments show that an LLM evaluator will frequently favor its own text generations over alternatives that human raters judge to be equally good [@PanicksseryEtAl2024SelfPreference]. While that specific result concerns the evaluation of generated text and doesn't establish a universal same-family bias when a model critiques RTL, simulator traces, timing reports, or physical-design results, Knight and Leveson's broader lesson still governs our core architecture claims.

The missing-property case presents an entirely different challenge. As we saw with Spectre and Meltdown, vulnerabilities often exploit microarchitectural side effects that our ordinary functional correctness constraints simply ignore [@LippEtAl2018Meltdown; @KocherEtAl2019Spectre]. Throwing more functional tests at ordinary program outputs would never have settled the confidentiality requirement. To support a robust security claim, we must design tests specifically targeting side-channel leakage, recognizing that our ordinary performance suites are entirely blind to these issues.

Furthermore, our checks themselves need checks. We use mutation testing to inject faults and rigorously report which ones a given suite successfully detects [@DeMilloLiptonSayward1978Hints]. However, a mutation score tells us something only about that specific injected fault model, meaning we must carefully handle any equivalent or unobservable mutants. When dealing with model-generated assertions and testbenches, we must ensure our chosen fault set closely resembles the kinds of errors the generator actually makes in practice, rather than relying solely on traditional hand-written mistakes.

We often find that a check can be perfectly valid for the property it observes, yet remain merely a proxy for our true architecture objective. Functional simulation might establish strict agreement for tested inputs without ever settling our performance questions, just as a cycle estimate might help us rank candidates without ever establishing final timing closure. For us as architects, the remaining question is always how far our cheaper observations can reliably carry our stronger, system-level claims.

As reviewers, we can support a technical conclusion only after our project rigorously maps the identified material requirements, qualifies all supporting artifacts and results, resolves uncertainties relative to our strict acceptance margins, and deploys a sufficiently different failure path whenever the consequence warrants it. Since our requirement set may still be incomplete, we must explicitly retain any residual unknowns and nonclaims as a core part of our final conclusion. Ultimately, this hard-won technical support does not authorize blind architecture commitment; rather, it establishes exactly which next technical action our feedback can legitimately justify.
## Routing the Next Technical Action

Once our qualified result supports, contradicts, or leaves a specific architectural claim unresolved, the feedback naturally points us to the design object needing attention and our next eligible technical action. The feedback signal doesn't prescribe its own design update, just as a single technical action doesn't authorize a final architecture commitment on its own.

If we encounter an incomplete or invalid execution record, we route it directly back to the tool environment for debugging, long before we attempt verification or feedback. For our remaining cross-cutting statuses, we direct our attention straight to the architectural object implicated by the qualified or verified result (@tbl-feedback-destinations). Formal statuses rely on the more specific actions we've defined in @tbl-formal-result-status.

| **Established status** | **Object needing attention** | **Resulting move** |
|  –  |  –  |  –  |
| **Invalid execution** | Tool-connected environment | Repair our extraction, state, lineage, or invocation before interpreting the design candidate. |
| **Wrong represented state** | Design representation | Correct our represented problem and invalidate results that relied on the wrong state. |
| **Qualified architecture effect** | Project record; design owner if revision is supported | Record our bounded result and revise the architecture only when it supports that move. |
| **Proxy outside support** | Approach choice or qualification study | Recalibrate, narrow, replace, or stop using our proxy. We do not create training labels automatically. |
| **Missing constraint or assumption** | Study formulation or representation | Record our rationale and repair the architectural object that omitted the requirement. |
| **Resolved outcome, unresolved mechanism** | Study formulation | Preserve our result and add a distinguishing contrast before using the explanation to guide another design change. |
| **Unresolved comparison** | Measurement plan or study formulation | Improve our contrast, precision target, observation budget, or stopping rule. |
| **Difference below the decision margin** | Project record | Preserve our result without forcing an architecture or model update. |
| **Accepted bounded exception** | Project record and responsible owner | Preserve our failed status, scope, rationale, compensating control, residual risk, expiration, and reopening condition. |

: **Established status determines our next technical move.** Execution failure routes directly to our tool environment before verification or feedback. Our qualified or verified results then direct repair, recording, revision, requalification, or no change at the relevant architectural object.
{#tbl-feedback-destinations tbl-colwidths="[32,25,43]"}

Our qualification process can point either to the architecture object needing repair or to the one ready to use the result, while leaving any unsupported inferences open. Importantly, this direction doesn't mandate a design change. If we see a difference below our declared decision margin, we simply update the project record; if we land a proof, it discharges only its explicitly stated property; and if we grant a waiver, we preserve the failure as a strictly scoped exception. Under no circumstances does our routing turn a tool failure or an unresolved architectural comparison into an automated training label.

::: {.callout-field-note title="An illustrative timing return produces a bounded action"}
**The expectation.** Our qualified timing return should support a bounded claim and an eligible repair, rather than jumping to a broad conclusion about the entire processor pipeline.

**In practice.** This example serves as an illustration, rather than empirical project evidence. For our mapped netlist `CPU-NL-17`, constraint set `CPU-SDC-17`, and corner `SS_0P72V_125C`, the return for path `EX-MEM-P17` reports $-0.04\,\mathrm{ns}$ setup slack from `U_EX/alu_sum_reg[17]/Q` to `U_MEM/addr_reg[17]/D`. Our complete tool status, constrained endpoints, clock model, derates, and report lineage qualify the value for that specific named setup check. Our bounded claim states strictly that this path violates its zero-slack setup requirement under the declared conditions. It tells us absolutely nothing about hold timing, functional correctness, power dissipation, behavior at another corner, or our global chip feasibility. That localized claim makes moving a pipeline boundary or reducing logic depth an eligible architectural move, which we must subsequently follow up with logical equivalence checks, functional regressions, and setup-and-hold reruns for every affected mode and corner.

**The lesson.** We must retain the failing path and its conditions alongside our repair rationale. We reopen this result whenever our netlist, constraint set, clock model, derates, or the affected path endpoints undergo any change.
:::

Securing a qualified status makes our next technical action eligible, but it doesn't automatically schedule our next attempt. For instance, an invalid execution permits our environment repair, a qualified hard-constraint violation permits candidate rejection or architecture revision, and an unresolved comparison permits us to seek a better measurement or contrast. We consider a retry eligible only when a linked attempt has a real chance to resolve our pending design decision within the remaining verification budget. While @sec-running-the-loop handles exactly how we schedule, repeat, budget, and stop these eligible actions, this chapter establishes what our architectural signal can actually justify. Fundamentally, structural defects that block validation or required correctness will always take absolute precedence over our optional performance refinements.

When our feedback sources appear to conflict, we must first align the architecture candidate, property, conditions, tool versions, and aggregation methods. Often, we find the signals concern entirely different scopes rather than directly contradicting a single claim. If they truly still conflict, we inspect our shared assumptions and known error directions, and then we choose a distinguishing check specifically targeted at the disputed property. When neither result cleanly supersedes the other, we preserve both as unresolved. We never simply average incompatible signals, nor do we select a source based purely on organizational prestige.

We treat a reviewer's observation strictly as feedback. Project approval, conversely, operates as a separate, authorized action. Neither mechanism can magically transform an unsupported result into a valid one. While an approval may accept a bounded residual risk for our design, it can never supply a missing measurement or bypass a necessary check. Our final architecture commitment remains a wholly separate milestone, which rightfully belongs in @sec-what-architect-owns.

We occasionally allow failed checks to remain open under a bounded waiver accepted by an authorized design owner. However, this waiver never turns a failed result into a passing grade. Instead, it explicitly retains our failed check, the rationale, the exact scope, the responsible owner, any compensating control, the residual risk, the expiration condition, and our specific reopening trigger. In physical-verification workflows, robust waiver support preserves waived design-rule violations and their associated metadata. For example, Siemens documents this exact behavior for Calibre Auto-Waivers, which successfully applies these records across our subsequent design rule checking (DRC) runs [@SiemensCalibreAutoWaivers]. While the technical record firmly belongs here, the ultimate authority to accept that residual risk resides with @sec-what-architect-owns.

The intensive work of qualifying a technical return divides neatly into two halves, and we can only hand one of those halves to an automated harness. Once we declare our conditions, a harness can seamlessly check that a return parses correctly, that its parsed entries carry proper physical units, that its lineage binds back to a valid request, that two experimental arms ran under matched conditions, and which regressions a recent change makes worth rerunning. However, determining whether a property accurately expresses our requirement, whether a comparator is genuinely fair, and whether a proposed mechanism actually produced the observed effect – these remain fundamental architecture questions that a harness can merely record, but never settle. As faster design generation adds more of both kinds of work, our harness eagerly absorbs the former. The latter, representing our core engineering judgment, stays exactly where it always was.

Ultimately, our routing process ends with an eligible technical action. A qualified result transforms into true architectural learning only when it actively changes our current run or project, or leaves a durable lesson that our future design work retains.
## How Returned Signals Change the Work

We often see feedback paths that stay tightly confined within a current simulation or synthesis run. When our tools flag a qualified SRAM access-time violation, for instance, we can immediately trigger a predeclared no-dispatch action for that specific cache candidate. From there, we can dynamically pivot – perhaps by evaluating a smaller cache array, fundamentally revising the memory organization, or simply pruning that design branch altogether using the run controls we detailed in @sec-running-the-loop.

Other results inevitably outlive a single run and fundamentally alter our overall project state. Consider an interface counterexample that we have rigorously reviewed and proven realizable under intended operating conditions. We use this discovery to permanently add a retained protocol constraint and a new regression test. It allows us to correct our represented state, withdraw qualification from any affected component, and explicitly record which future interface changes might reopen our earlier architectural conclusions.

Crucially, a powerful result often remains highly useful long after our current project tapes out. We can preserve the qualified range, the held-out checks, and even the failed corner cases for a cache proxy model as meticulously scoped artifacts and hard-won lessons. While our next generation of projects might reuse these assets, we must always re-establish our core conclusions under the strict transfer conditions described in @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack.

However, we must recognize that none of these updates – whether to the run, the project state, or our retained lessons – constitutes an automatic model update. Project learning and machine learning are fundamentally different beasts in our domain. A newly discovered design constraint, a contradicted performance comparison, or a newly validated mechanism can easily update our project state without ever acting as valid training data. To properly update a learned model, we need a clearly named target, rigorously usable labels, a strictly defined scope, and a robust acceptance test. We cannot simply reduce tool failures, unmatched simulation results, or unresolved comparisons into naive pass-or-fail labels for a training pipeline.

As computer architects, we already maintain extensive verification plans, deep requirements traceability, comprehensive regression and coverage databases, final signoff reports, waiver records, and precise change-impact tracking. Our cumulative study record simply indexes these existing mechanisms, linking them directly to the engineering claims and design decisions they support. We use it to unify our understanding, not to impose a parallel workflow or add another layer of unnecessary bureaucracy.

### Updating a Learned Component

We must treat any updated model or proxy as an entirely new component version within our broader design system [@SculleyEtAl2015Hidden]. In computer architecture, rolling out that version change can instantly invalidate our candidate rankings, break our proxy scopes, and corrupt cached search decisions that relied on the previous component's behavior. Furthermore, because our architecture search actively chooses which design candidates receive computationally expensive labels, our labeled outcomes are strictly policy-selected; the missing outcomes are never truly random. While active learning studies how a generic method chooses which example to label next [@Settles2009ActiveLearning], we introduced the corresponding selective-acquisition problem for architecture data in @sec-data-representations-world-models. If we learn only from the labels our search returns, we risk reinforcing the exact design regions our current methodology already favors, permanently preserving its blind spots.

Before we allow this updated component back into our active design process, we must rigorously record the update data, the acquisition policy, and our retained selection decisions – especially documenting those design candidates that did not receive labels. We then push the project to test failure-relevant cases alongside previously qualified strata that we explicitly held out of the update. We systematically repeat our decision-relevant error bounds, ranking validations, and proxy-qualification checks while hunting for unexpected regressions. Wherever practical, we should deploy randomized or stratified audit evaluations to probe the architectural space far outside our policy's default choices.

If we allow our acceptance results to continuously steer subsequent model updates, that repeated exposure turns our evaluation cases into mere development data, much like how adaptive reuse can dangerously overfit a holdout set [@DworkEtAl2015ReusableHoldout]. Therefore, we must deliberately keep our acceptance cases untouched or regularly refresh them. We should quarantine the newly updated component outside our active pipeline until it confidently passes a shadow evaluation – one that in no way steers our candidate selection – or clears a highly independent acceptance path. Only then does it reenter our flow, carrying a freshly revised qualification scope and updated reopening conditions, rather than blindly inheriting its predecessor's scope. Crucially, while passing these checks qualifies the new version for its declared use, it absolutely does not inherit the specific architectural conclusions supported by the older version.

### Reopening and Requalifying

We constantly face moments where we must reopen an old interpretation because changing conditions demand full requalification. A shifted workload, a new software image, an updated toolchain, a revised operating condition, or even a contrary experimental observation can instantly reopen our dependent architectural claims – without predetermining what the next revision will look like. When this happens, we must precisely identify which bindings or structural relationships no longer hold true. We do not simply throw our hands up and silently invalidate unrelated simulation results.

We encounter distribution shift whenever the data-generating conditions we face in actual use diverge from those we represented during initial development or qualification [@QuinoneroCandelaEtAl2009DatasetShift]. In high-performance architecture design, this shift might manifest as a drastically new workload mix, a pivot into an unexplored candidate region, or a completely new distribution of process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) conditions. We define a *drift signal* as any observed degradation over time across these conditions – or within our proxy's residuals, interval coverage, or ranking stability. While this signal is a critical warning, it does not identify its own root cause, nor does it automatically authorize a costly retraining cycle.

Fortunately, many of these changes remain neatly contained within our current project and target decision space. An aggressively tightened timing constraint might reopen only the specific requirement comparisons and margins that relied on the old limit; a fully qualified timing measurement can remain perfectly intact if its underlying artifact and PVT conditions haven't budged. Similarly, rolling out a revised reset sequence or interface version might reopen the functional, formal, and integration checks that directly consume it, while leaving our unrelated power or area measurements untouched. We must rigorously trace every claim and check back to its driving workload, toolset, artifact, operating condition, interface, and formal requirement. We then rerun only the minimum adequate set of affected checks, keeping an unaffected claim alive only when we can attach a solidly recorded rationale.

Any mismatch in our candidate, configuration, toolchain, or operating condition can quickly render an affected execution record stale, forcing us to perform lineage repair or rerun the exact same check. Furthermore, shifting workload populations, degraded phase coverage, or aggressive movement among our design candidates might require completely new sampling strategies and repeated qualification. If we observe deteriorating proxy-reference residuals, collapsing interval coverage, or wildly unstable rankings, we may have no choice but to narrow, recalibrate, replace, or entirely halt the proxy. Relearning the model is only one possible response – and it is only viable when the proxy is a true learned component backed by a robust, independent acceptance test.

Finally, we face a genuinely new target decision only when our objective's meaning, the legal architectural action space, the artifact boundary, or the acceptance semantics shift enough to fundamentally alter the decision itself. Determining exactly which prior results safely carry over into this new target becomes a complex transfer problem, rather than a simple selective requalification within our current decision boundaries (@sec-loop-patterns-across-stack). Until we explicitly cross that boundary, we preserve every historical result alongside its well-defined scope, name all affected dependencies and minimum adequate checks, and firmly let the new empirical evidence drive our next update.
## Common Pitfalls

As computer architects, we often misinterpret the vital signals we receive from our feedback loops and verification checks, leading us toward fundamentally incorrect design decisions and flawed models. When evaluating microarchitectural candidates, we frequently stumble into a few classic traps – particularly when interpreting tool returns, over-relying on proxy metrics, and reusing validation data:

- **Treating execution failure as candidate failure:** When we encounter a setup, license, invocation, or parse error, it simply means our measurement path broke down. If we automatically reject a candidate architecture or use that system crash as a negative training label, we create a false negative. Our underlying hardware design might be perfectly sound; it is merely our simulation or synthesis environment that failed.
- **Overextending a proxy's valid range:** We might successfully optimize an early-stage IPC, energy, wirelength, or congestion estimate, only to discover that we have inadvertently degraded our post-route power, performance, and area (PPA), our silicon correctness, or our real-workload objectives. We must remember that a proxy metric remains valid only within its rigorously qualified range. Before we finalize any major architectural decision, we have to validate our early proxy results against later, more comprehensive sign-off tools.
- **Reusing adaptation feedback as acceptance evidence:** If we repeatedly recycle a holdout set or reuse specific labels to tune our architecture, we can easily trick ourselves into thinking our design models are improving. In reality, this practice merely bakes in our existing blind spots, destroying the diagnostic value of the evidence we are reusing. To guarantee true architectural robustness, we must ensure our acceptance evidence remains strictly unseen throughout the entire adaptation phase.
## Open Questions

The mechanisms we rely on to qualify tool returns and validate proxy metrics highlight a stark boundary between established engineering practice and active architecture research. As we have seen throughout this chapter, qualifying feedback demands that we tightly bound the uncertainty and scope of every measurement. Yet, modern architectural studies increasingly depend on learned heuristics, generated assertions, and multi-fidelity approximations that blur these very bounds. The frontier of our discipline lies precisely at this intersection. When we can no longer afford exhaustive formal checks or direct cycle-accurate measurements, our primary barrier to sound decision-making becomes establishing the sufficiency of a proxy or uncovering correlated blind spots across ostensibly independent tools. We cannot dismiss these challenges as mere implementation details to be patched over with ad-hoc scripts. Instead, they represent fundamental gaps in how we evaluate complex computing systems. Restoring rigor to architecture evaluation remains a critical target for dedicated PhD theses and sustained research programs.

### Qualifying Proxies and Checks

A fast or seemingly independent check only holds value when we thoroughly understand its scope, its blind spots, and its reliance on other checks.

- **Proxy sufficiency:** How do we pinpoint when a proxy is accurate enough to safely steer a design decision? We often see proxies that boast low average error, yet they can still misrank candidates or obscure severe constraint violations right at the decision boundary. Our unresolved challenge is determining exactly when a proxy's error distorts the overarching architectural conclusion, and knowing precisely when we must invoke a stronger, computationally expensive check.

- **Measuring correlated failure:** How can we detect when our varied checks harbor the exact same blind spots? Different architectural simulation tools, analytical models, and even human reviewers can unwittingly inherit identical specification errors, workload gaps, or training biases. If our checks share a root cause of failure, their agreement offers us nothing but false comfort. Our open problem is formally identifying the dependencies that threaten our architectural claims, allowing us to know exactly when we must invest in a genuinely independent observation path.

- **Checking generated assertions:** How do we go about verifying our verification artifacts? Our generated tests and assertions might be syntactically flawless and mathematically nonvacuous, yet they can still completely ignore critical protocol behaviors, complex timing interactions, reset sequences, or forward progress guarantees. We must discover how to definitively prove that a generated property is robust enough to anchor our intended architecture claim, rather than just settling for an artifact that is merely capable of producing a passing result.

### Learning and Requalifying Feedback

Even our qualified results suffer from bias based on which design candidates we initially checked, and they can rapidly grow stale as project conditions evolve.

- **Updating learned components:** How do we stop our learned models from structurally reinforcing their own blind spots? An AI-assisted architecture exploration system typically only observes outcomes for the candidates that its own search policy favors. Over time, this selective feedback entrenches the design regions the system already prefers, while actively obscuring critical, unexplored failures. Although we can inject independent sampling, we still face the open question of how heavily we can safely lean on fast, policy-driven feedback when our definitive, heavy-duty architectural checks are severely delayed or computationally prohibitive.

- **Selecting adequate reruns:** When conditions inevitably change, how do we isolate the absolute minimum set of checks necessary to requalify our claims? A seemingly trivial design tweak can silently invalidate a cascade of prior results, yet we rarely map the full web of dependencies across artifacts, measurements, and formal checks. If we simply rerun everything, we squander invaluable simulation compute and implementation time. Conversely, if our impact analysis is incomplete, we leave stale, unsupported architectural claims intact in our methodology. Our ongoing challenge is to systematically deduce the most compact set of renewed checks that safely reestablishes the foundation for our affected claims.
## Conclusion {#sec-trust-boundary-conclusion}

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Stronger claims require stronger checks"}
We must explicitly match our verification checks to the specific properties and consequences of our architectural claims. True verification strength arises from property-appropriate fidelity and coverage, a sufficiently independent observation path where shared failures matter, appropriate calibration, and bounded uncertainty relative to our decision margins. It does not automatically stem from simply using a more expensive simulation tool or waiting for a later stage in our design flow. Without these essential qualities, agreement across tools can merely preserve a shared blind spot, or a highly precise result might ultimately settle the wrong architectural property. We can rely on cheaper, faster checks for reversible design space exploration within explicitly stated limits, but we must mandate additional, rigorous verification before drawing high-consequence architectural conclusions.
:::

Once we qualify an architectural result at an appropriate strength, we must apply a different rule to determine how our team leverages that insight.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Only let qualified results drive the next architecture action"}
A raw simulation or analytical return remains completely unusable until we establish exactly what ran, identify the specific candidate and property it evaluates, and clearly define the design, workload, and tool conditions. Only then do we understand the comparative or formal claim it supports. We must route only these carefully qualified results to drive an execution repair, a design revision, an additional check, a retained architectural lesson, or a technical stop. If we route an unqualified return, we risk repairing the wrong hardware module, revising an unsupported design candidate, or preserving a false lesson in our methodology. We should trace every architectural action back to the specific result that justified it, explicitly noting its limits and reopening conditions. When design conditions inevitably change, we must proactively reopen the affected result rather than silently widening its original scope.
:::

As computer architects, we can translate a returned signal into a bounded, actionable result only after we rigorously establish execution and artifact validity, qualify the relevant measurement or formal status, and match our checks directly to our architectural claims. That qualification status directly dictates which technical actions remain eligible for our design. We retaining the core result alongside its rationale, limits, and reopening conditions, we build a robust foundation for ongoing architectural learning.

While qualification determines which design actions are logically eligible, any multi-step architectural study must still determine precisely when to schedule and stop those actions without losing critical state, cost data, lineage, or underlying rationale. In @sec-running-the-loop, we explain how to orchestrate these complex decisions throughout our design cycles.
